description_full: Corporación América Airports S.A., through its subsidiaries, acquires, develops, and operates airport concessions. It operates 52 airports in Latin America, Europe, and Eurasia. The company was formerly known as A.C.I. Airports International S.à r.l. and changed its name to Corporación América Airports S.A. in September 2017. The company was founded in 1998 and is based in Luxembourg, Luxembourg. Corporación América Airports S.A. operates as a subsidiary of A.C.I. Airports S.à r.l.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 6K people. Revenue per employee of $311K ranks in the below the sector median among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $71K of free cash flow annually.
financial_summary: Corporacion America Airports SA is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.1B market cap on $2.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +12% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 32%.

The business throws off $449M in free cash flow — roughly 23 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.81× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 80% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 25% operating margin runs 16pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.24x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.67, it is more defensive than the market.
About $6.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 74% in the 2020 crash and 24% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 68% below its DCF fair value of $78.24, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 36%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $59.92 to $104 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 14.0 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 5.9 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 9.1 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 82% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 11.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $32.40 on average, 30% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.8%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.04).
It runs a 32% gross margin and converts 23% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.81x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.8x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 9pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($860.8M of cash against $1.1B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.0x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.5% over 3 years and 26.4% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 41%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 11.1% on average.
Analysts expect 18.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 79.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 16%.
people: With about 6,300 employees, each generates about $311K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 2.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $71K of free cash flow per employee.
